v: CHAPTER VIII · THE KITCHEN AT ELEVEN

If a man could stand at a distance of eleven years from a Tuesday in November and look back down the length of it, if he could see the kitchen and the pan left soaking in the sink and the woman sitting on the counter with her heels knocking against the cupboard door, if he could hear again the story she was telling about a girl from her school who married a man that collected clocks, a story with no point to it, told for no reason except that the hour was late and she was warm and he was there to be told it, if he could see all of this and know, as he watches, that the man in the kitchen is not listening properly, that he is filling the kettle and half-composing his reply and letting the whole thing go past him because it is ordinary and because ordinary things arrive with the promise of repetition folded inside them, if he could see the man about to lose what he is standing inside of, and could not reach him, could not put a hand on his shoulder and turn him around, what would he do with such a vantage? What use is a distance that only shows you the thing and never returns you to it?
She stops in the middle of the clock story. She does that.

She says his name. Not a question, not the beginning of a sentence, only the name, the way you say a name to find out whether someone is still in the room with you or has drifted off behind his own eyes. And he looks up from the kettle. And she is looking at him. And nothing else happens.
Nothing else happens.

A second, perhaps a second and a half. No message is passed between them. If someone had stopped the clock at that instant and asked him what she was telling him he would have had nothing to give, because she was telling him nothing, because there was nothing to tell, because she was only there, uncovered, for a second and a half, and he was there too.
A second and a half. Eleven years have not exhausted it.
Man in the kitchen. You with the kettle in your hand. Turn around.

He does not turn around. He was never going to turn around. Whatever this is that reaches toward him from eleven years off, it does not arrive, it has never once arrived, it arrives at the page instead and stops there, which is the only place it was ever going to arrive.

So the letter is written to a man who cannot receive it. What sort of letter is that? Not a warning, since he will do it all regardless. Not a confession, since he has done nothing yet. Call it what it is: a hand laid on a shoulder in a room the hand cannot enter.
And still it gets written. Every year, in some form, it gets written.

Would it have helped him to know? Lay it all before him that night, the calendar, the fourth November, the exact shape of the silence that comes after. What then? He holds her differently and she feels it. She asks what is wrong. There is an answer or there is a lie, and either way the kitchen stops being a kitchen and becomes the site of something, and the girl who married the man who collected clocks is never mentioned, because a story with no point cannot survive being told in a room where something is happening.
The pointlessness was not a flaw in that evening. It was the evening.

Seven chapters, and a wall at the end of every road. Approach it by measurement: refused. Approach it by proof, and the proof turns and seals the man who made it. Approach it by love, and love is converted into an inventory of a body's weight. Approach it by foresight, and foresight hands you the whole road and no wheel. Every crossing catalogued, every failure exact.
In the kitchen there was no wall.

There is no argument that will make that believable and none will be offered. For a second and a half, at eleven at night, between two people attempting nothing whatsoever, the thing that cannot be crossed was not there. Not overcome. Not approached and understood. Absent.
He did not notice. She did not notice. There was a kettle to fill.
There is a second kitchen, older than that one, and a woman in it who is not her.

She is standing at a stove with her back to a boy who is doing his homework at the table, and she is asking him something about his day, and he is answering in the way boys answer, which is not at all. This happens perhaps four thousand times. Four thousand is a conservative figure. The single most repeated event of his childhood, and he could not, at gunpoint, produce one specific instance of it.
Ask him about the day his grandfather died and he can give you the weather.

The mind keeps what is singular and discards what recurs, which is an efficient policy and a catastrophic one, since the things that recur are the things that were actually one's life. He has, in total, four or five hours of his mother that survive as memory. She was present for eighteen years. The arithmetic is not consoling.

And the four thousand askings are not gone in the way a lost object is gone, where a better search recovers it. They were never recorded. They passed through him at the time and were spent at the time, as they should have been, as air is spent.

Here is the part that should be said carefully, since it can be made to sound like a moral and it is not one: she was not asking to obtain information. Neither was the girl on the counter telling a story about clocks in order to convey the story. The clock-collector was a vehicle. The question about his day was a vehicle. What was being transmitted in both cases was the same thing, which has no content and cannot be summarized and does not survive being written down, and which he has spent his adult life failing to name and will not name now.
His mother is alive. This should be said, since the whole passage has been written in the tense of the dead and she is in fact at this moment sixty-one and probably standing at that stove.
Which raises the question that will not leave him alone: why does he write about her as though she were gone?

Because the four thousand askings are gone. Because whatever he had access to, at eight years old, at that table, with his homework and his half-answers, is not accessible now, and cannot be recovered by driving four hours to see her, which he does, and does not regret, and which is not the same. The mother in the second kitchen is not the mother at the stove. He can reach the one. The other is behind him, at a distance of thirty years, asking about his day.
You may call it grief if you like. He has stopped objecting to the word. It seems a strange thing to grieve for someone who telephones on Sundays.
"You never listen to a word I say."
She said that, on the counter, in the kitchen at eleven, and she said it laughing, and it was true, and she did not mean it as an accusation because she thought there was time.
Consider the man who wishes to safeguard an evening.

He sees what it is worth. He is not a fool; he understands, sitting there, that this is the good part, that the years will not improve on a Tuesday like this one, and he resolves that this evening shall not be lost. So he sets himself to attend. He looks carefully at her face. He notices the light and the sound of the heels on the cupboard door, and he thinks: I am inside the best hour of my life and I will not squander it.
He has just squandered it.

The looking-carefully is not being-there. It is a man standing slightly outside an evening taking an inventory of it, and the inventory is not the evening, and while he compiles it she is talking to someone who has left the room. She feels the leaving. She cannot name it, and later, at a distance of some months, when they are arguing about something unrelated, she will say that he was never really in it with her, and he will not know what she means, and he will be able to produce the details of that Tuesday in evidence against her, every one of them accurate.
He will win that argument. He remembers the shirt she was wearing.
So there are two ways to lose an hour and no third.

Fail to attend, and it goes past you unmarked and unrecoverable, four thousand times. Attend deliberately, and you step out of it in the act of attending, and take home a record instead of an evening.

Between these, in a very narrow place, is what happened for a second and a half at the kettle: no attention, no record, no distance whatsoever between him and it. Nobody has ever managed to do that on purpose.
"Are you even here right now."
"Don't write about me."
She said that once, seriously, not laughing, when she found out what he did in the evenings. He agreed. He knows perfectly well what this chapter is.

The defence he would offer, if she asked for one, is that nothing here would identify her to anyone who did not already know, and that the woman on the counter is not her but a version of her assembled out of what survived, which is precisely the four minutes and not the eleven hundred days, and that the difference between those two women is the whole subject of the chapter and also the reason she was right to ask.
A poor defence. He is making it anyway.
There is an argument that all of this is simply what time does, and that a man complaining about it is complaining that water is wet.

Take the argument seriously, since it is the strongest one against everything written here. Nothing described in this chapter is unusual. Every person alive has lost the ordinary hours and kept the wrong photographs. No mechanism has failed. The apparatus is working exactly as designed, and to call the ordinary operation of memory a wound is sentimental, and the sentimentality is a young man's, and he will grow out of it.
Grant all of it. And notice what has been granted.

That the standard equipment of a human being includes an inability to retain the parts of a life that were worth living. That this is normal. That everyone you pass on the street is carrying four minutes of the person they loved most and has stopped remarking on it. The argument does not soften the fact. It generalises it, which is worse, and then asks you to be calm about it on the grounds that everyone else is calm about it.
He is not calm about it, and holds that position with more confidence than any other in this book.

The knight of measurement would call this a defeat and file it. Something occurred; it cannot be reproduced; it cannot be induced; the mechanism is unavailable to inspection. Under his method that is a closed case with a null result.
But watch what the method has done. The only event in these pages where the wall was absent has been marked insufficiently documented.

About the documentation he is not wrong. The trouble lies in what he counts as an outcome. A man who requires that a thing be repeatable before he will admit that it happened has made a rule which excludes, at a stroke, every single moment of his life that was worth having, each of which occurred once, in a specific kitchen, on a Tuesday, and none of which he can produce on demand.
A question worth putting to anyone who has loved somebody: what do you actually have of them?

Not what do you remember. What do you have. Take an inventory and be honest about the results. A handful of photographs, most of them posed and therefore useless. Some anecdotes worn smooth from retelling, which have long since replaced the events they describe. A few sentences she said that you can still hear in her voice, and here you should be careful, because you cannot verify the voice, and the voice is the part you would most want to be sure of.
Perhaps four minutes of genuine footage in total.

Against which: eleven hundred days. She was in the same building as him for something over eleven hundred days. Where are they? Not misplaced. Not filed somewhere awaiting retrieval. Gone in the manner of water poured on ground, which does not go anywhere in particular and cannot be gathered up.

And the four minutes that survive were not selected for merit. That is the thing that ought to be disturbing and never is. Memory did not sit down at the end and choose the best of it. It kept a bad photograph from a wedding they attended and did not keep the morning she was ill and he brought her something and she looked up at him. He knows that morning happened. He cannot see it. The wedding photograph he can see, and he does not want it, and there is no exchange rate.
There was a period, in the second year, when he began writing things down.

Not a journal, nothing so orderly. Fragments on his phone, late, while she slept: what she said at dinner, a way she had of pronouncing a certain word, the specific complaint she made about her sister. He had noticed the erosion by then and he was doing what a sensible man does about erosion, which is to build.
The file still exists. He has it open now.

The file is unreadable. Not sentimentally difficult, but unreadable in the sense that the entries are notes to a person who was already present at the events and therefore required only a trigger, and that person no longer exists, and the trigger fires nothing. "The thing with the umbrella." He has no idea what the thing with the umbrella was. "Told me about the dog on the beach." No dog surfaces. Forty entries and perhaps six of them still open onto anything at all.
He wrote them so that this would not happen. They are the proof that it happened.

And here is the joke buried in it, which took him some years to see: the entries he can still read are the ones he wrote badly, in a hurry, with too much detail and no shape. The ones he took care over, the ones he crafted, are the sealed ones. Craft was already a step outside. The careless entries were dictation and the careful ones were composition, and composition, it turns out, is a form of leaving the room.
Toward the end, in the last of the four autumns, they had an argument in a car about a hotel booking.

The details are available. He can supply them. What he wants recorded here is not the argument but a thing that happened after it, at a service station, where she went in to buy water and came back with two bottles and handed him one without looking at him, still angry, and he took it, still angry, and they drank the water in the car in silence for a minute and a half before starting again.
That minute and a half was the same as the second and a half in the kitchen.

He did not notice it then either. Eleven years on he can find no difference between them except duration and the fact that the second one came at the end. Two people, no attempt at anything, no message, no wall.
The last one arrived in the middle of a fight over a hotel and was carried out to the car in a plastic bottle.
He was not paying attention. That was never the tragedy of it.

The tragedy, if the word is even usable here, is that paying attention would not have helped, and that he has needed eleven years to work out something a less careful man understands at twenty-five: the good hours are not stored anywhere. They cannot be banked against a later shortage. They are spent as they occur, and the spending is the whole of their function, and a life goes past this way at the rate of one hour per hour whether one is watching it or not.
She is somewhere tonight. The counter is in another flat now, with other people's cups on it. His mother is at the stove.

And a man at a distance of eleven years, who can see all of it and reach none of it, sets this down and finds, at the end of a chapter written to say what could not be said at the time, that there was nothing to say at the time.
That was the point. She was on the counter, and he was at the kettle, and the pan was in the sink, and it was enough, and no one had to know it was enough for it to be enough.
